title: The pricing race
summary: Price a European call three ways — formula, Monte Carlo, ideal quantum amplitude estimation — and read the resource bill.

shots.title:
The pricing
race.
shots.subtitle: One option. A formula, a simulation, and a quantum algorithm.
shots.narration: Time to use what we've learned on a real finance problem: pricing an option.

shots.text: A **call option** is the right to buy at a strike price **K** on a date **T**. Its payoff: $\max(S_T - K,\ 0)$.
shots.narration: A call option is the right to buy an asset at a fixed strike price on a future date. If the price ends above the strike you gain the difference. Otherwise, nothing.

notes: Black–Scholes (1973): a closed-form price for simple European options.
Nobel memorial prize, 1997 — and our benchmark today.
shots.narration: For simple European options there's a famous closed-form answer, the Black–Scholes formula from 1973, honoured with a Nobel memorial prize in 1997. It will be our ground truth.

shots.text: Real desks trade **exotics** with no formula. So they **simulate**: thousands of random price paths, average the discounted payoffs.
shots.narration: But real desks trade exotic derivatives with no neat formula. So they simulate: thousands of random price paths, average the payoffs, discount to today. That's Monte Carlo.

Monte Carlo's error falls like one over root N. Ideal amplitude estimation falls like one over N. On a log chart, one line is twice as steep. For high precision, that's the difference between millions and thousands of evaluations.

nodes.label: Load price distribution on n qubits

shots.narration: The quantum recipe has three stages. Load a discretised distribution of future prices onto n qubits. Encode the payoff as the probability of one extra qubit. Then run amplitude estimation on that probability.

shots.label: **logical** qubits estimated for useful advantage in derivative pricing
shots.context: Goldman Sachs & IBM, 2021 · T-depth 54 million · must run in about a second
shots.narration: Then the bill. A 2021 study by Goldman Sachs and IBM estimated that beating classical pricing on their benchmark derivatives would need about eight thousand logical qubits, a T-depth of fifty-four million, and the whole run done in about a second.

shots.heading: Why it's hard
items: **Loading** the distribution costs gates — it can eat the speed-up
Markets move: a price that takes an hour is worthless
shots.narration: Why so demanding? Loading the distribution costs gates and can eat the speed-up. The deep circuits need error-corrected logical qubits. And a price that arrives after the market has moved is worthless.

shots.text: Researchers are shaving the bill with **lower-depth** variants of amplitude estimation — trading some speed-up for feasibility.
shots.narration: Researchers are shaving that bill with lower-depth versions of amplitude estimation that skip the costliest step, trading some of the speed-up for something buildable.

shots.text: Now race them yourself. Same option, three methods, an **honest scoreboard**.
shots.narration: Now race them yourself. Same option, the formula, Monte Carlo, and an ideal quantum estimator, with an honest scoreboard and the fine print beside it.

questions.prompt: With Monte Carlo, to cut the error from $0.10 to $0.01, how many times more paths do you need?
questions.explain: Error ∝ 1/√N: 10× smaller error needs 10² = 100× more paths.

questions.prompt: With ideal amplitude estimation, 10× smaller error needs roughly…
questions.explain: Error ∝ 1/N, so 10× precision costs about 10× the calls.

questions.prompt: What did the 2021 Goldman Sachs–IBM study estimate useful pricing advantage would need?
options: About 8,000 logical qubits and a T-depth of 54 million, run in about a second
questions.explain: From the published paper (Quantum, 2021). Earlier preprint drafts quoted 7.5k.
